strengths: The paper offers a useful empirical contribution to vision-language research by examining how language composition changes the information available about the same images. This has practical relevance to caption collection, dataset filtering, and multilingual evaluation.

The reported semantic-coverage trend appears across human annotations and two captioning systems. Table 1 reports increases from 2.98 to 4.35 objects and from 1.77 to 2.94 relations when comparing monolingual and multilingual averages. Comparing equal-sized caption sets addresses the basic confound of simply collecting more captions.

The Visual Genome evaluation provides valuable grounding: English–French–Chinese captions increase annotated-object coverage from 9.6% to 11.7% for Vertex and from 9.5% to 12.0% for LLaVA (Table 3). The supplementary study with 20 English/Japanese speakers provides additional human evidence.

The authors make meaningful efforts to validate their methodology, including translation assessment by 15 speakers, an alternative multilingual-embedding analysis, and fine-tuning experiments on held-out images. The distinction between semantic content and expression also makes the research questions accessible.
weaknesses: Consequential reporting inconsistencies weaken confidence in the quantitative evidence. All 36 entries in Table 14, labeled as LLaVA fine-tuning results, exactly reproduce the corresponding Vertex submatrix in Table 4, leaving the claimed independent replication unclear. Table 2 reports a Vertex monolingual attribute average of 1.98, although its seven entries average approximately 1.69; this affects the headline aggregate attribute improvement. These reliability concerns are a principal reason for the borderline assessment despite the consistent coverage trend.

The semantic measurements need stronger validation. Scene-graph parsing and concept merging determine what counts as additional information, but their accuracy and sensitivity are not evaluated. Caption length is not controlled, so greater coverage does not isolate differences in visual salience from differences in verbosity. Visual Genome object recall supports genuine additional content, but it does not establish the correctness of the additional relations and attributes.

The expressive conclusions are less secure than the semantic findings. Human translation evaluation primarily checks factual preservation, whereas translation can change tone, authenticity, and other stylistic properties. LIWC measurements are not validated for these short translated captions. Near-chance language prediction with one embedding-based classifier does not establish that translation artifacts are absent, and the untranslated embedding comparison retains the language biases acknowledged by the authors.

Some interpretations exceed what the experiments establish. Section 3.2 assumes that language switching within a model must induce less diversity than switching between models; no justified bound supports that assumption, so similar coverage cannot rule out language-specific model behavior. Fine-tuning primarily demonstrates adaptation to reference distributions, rather than improved visual representations. Even the matching-language advantage has exceptions: on Chinese XM references, multilingual training scores 0.131 versus 0.124 for Chinese training (Table 15).

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are incomplete. Exact model checkpoints, generation settings, graph-merging thresholds, and fine-tuning hyperparameters are insufficiently specified. The principal coverage and fine-tuning tables lack confidence intervals or variability across runs; the supplementary significance statements do not resolve this. These omissions matter particularly because the contribution rests on measured distributional differences and their interpretation.
